summary:
Brunei maintains a trans-specific offence under the Syariah Penal Code of a man posing as a woman or vice versa. The statute qualifies the conduct by acting without reasonable excuse or for immoral purposes.

A trans visitor cannot align documents with presentation. Brunei does not permit a person to change name or gender on official documents, and sex reassignment surgery is not allowed.

Enforcement is documented. On 11 March 2015 a civil servant was fined B$1,000 under the Syariah Penal Code Order for cross-dressing. A foreign government human rights report for 2017 recorded no known convictions under the cross-dressing ban that year and stated that morality provisions were enforced.

Same-sex sexual activity has been illegal in Brunei since 1906 under Straits Settlements law applied through the 1906 Courts Enactment as updated in 1908, and remained illegal after independence in 1984. Before 2019 implementation of the Syariah Penal Code Order, homosexual acts were punishable by up to 10 years imprisonment even if private and consensual.

From 2014 Brunei implemented the Syariah Penal Code Order 2013 in stages, with the final stage effective 3 April 2019. The Order bans liwat, defined as anal intercourse between men or between a man and a woman who is not his wife.

The de jure penalty for same-sex relations between men who are married is death by stoning, provided they admit to the acts or four adult male Muslim eyewitnesses testify to the acts. If that evidentiary standard is not met, the maximum penalty is seven years imprisonment and thirty strokes of whipping. For unmarried men the penalty is one year in prison or 100 lashes.

Sexual relations between women are punishable by any two of three stipulated penalties: caning of forty lashes, a maximum prison term of 10 years, and a fine of up to B$40,000.

Secular law separately criminalizes carnal intercourse against the order of nature. A July amendment to Chapter 22 of the Penal Code Order increased the minimum sentence to between 20 and 50 years incarceration, primarily applied in cases of rape or child abuse where both attacker and victim are male.

A moratorium on capital punishment affects the de jure stoning penalty. The Sultan stated the moratorium covers the new Shariah code. The government extended it to the Syariah Penal Code Order in May 2019. No execution has been carried out since 1957. A freshness check on 27 September 2026 found the moratorium intact and the 2019 code still in force. The moratorium remains revocable at any time by the absolute monarch with minimal process and without warning, and the seven-year and whipping penalty operates as the de facto penalty while it continues.

Scope for visitors is not assured. Reporting states the Syariah Penal Code mostly applies to Muslims, who comprise about two-thirds of the population. First-person reporting from April 2019 described a climate of fear with sources speaking anonymously and no assurance of non-enforcement against foreigners.

Protection is not reliable. LGBTI individuals reported intimidation by police, including threats to make their sexuality public.
tangentialFactors:
Global comparison places Brunei in a small group expressly criminalizing gender expression. An international human rights survey found at least 67 countries criminalise same-sex relations and at least nine criminalise gender expression. Brunei is one of at least two countries, with Oman, whose national laws expressly criminalise posing as or imitating a person of a different sex. Malaysia has a state-sharia analogue.

External bodies condemned the 2019 code. The United Nations and foreign governments condemned it. The UN High Commissioner urged Brunei to halt it. Human Rights Watch called it barbaric.

Bruneian society tends to associate homosexuality with effeminate men.

An additional offence risk is reported for conduct deemed to tarnish the image of Islam, which may be heavily punished. An international advocacy organisation has described Brunei as the country with the most worrisome state of rights for LGBT people in Southeast Asia.
localsOnly:
Residents cannot change name or gender on official documents, and sex reassignment surgery is not available.

Members of the lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intersex community reported unofficial and societal discrimination in public and private employment, housing, recreation and in obtaining services including education from state entities.

Members reported that the government monitored their activities and communications. Events on LGBTI topics were subject to restrictions on assembly and expression, with permits reportedly refused.

Reported police intimidation included threats to hamper obtaining a government job or to bar graduation from government academic institutions.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved as sourced: the precise current application of Syariah Penal Code provisions to non-Muslims and to short-term visitors is not fully specified in the sourced material beyond reporting that the law mostly applies to Muslims with no assurance of non-enforcement against foreigners.

Not sourced in this inventory: current frequency of prosecutions for cross-dressing after 2017. The 2017 report noted that sharia implementing regulations were still unissued at that time, and updated regulatory status was not sourced.
